title: Hypertension: diagnosis and outpatient management (India, InSH)
subject: cardiology
setting: Primary care, outpatient clinic, NCD clinic
summary: InSH 2025 defines stage 1 hypertension as 130 to 139/80 to 89 and stage 2 as 140/90 or more. Confirm with repeat office and out-of-office readings, start drugs at 140/90 (above 130/80 if high risk), begin with a low-dose two-drug single pill combination (ACEI or ARB with a CCB or thiazide), and treat most adults to below 130/80 mmHg.

sections.title: Classify and confirm
items: Normal below 120/80. Raised BP: systolic 120 to 129 with diastolic below 80. Stage 1 hypertension: 130 to 139 and/or 80 to 89 mmHg. Stage 2: 140 and/or 90 mmHg or more.
Screen every adult aged 18 and over opportunistically at every point of care; target community screening at the elderly (over 60), obese, smokers, diabetes and those with CVD or a family history.

Diagnose from at least 2 separate office visits 3 to 4 weeks apart. Use a validated automated upper-arm oscillometric device; measure at least 5 minutes after arrival, seated, arm at heart level, feet flat, and average 2 of 3 readings.

Measure both arms at the first visit and use the higher arm if the difference is consistently more than 10 mmHg; refer if more than 20 mmHg. Check standing BP at 1 and 3 minutes in the elderly, diabetes and anyone with postural symptoms.

Raised BP or stage 1 at a first visit: 7 days of home or ambulatory monitoring and review at 1 week, then lifestyle measures for at least 3 months. Out-of-office equivalents of office 140/90: home 135/85, daytime ABPM 135/85, night-time 120/70, 24-hour 130/80 mmHg.
Home BP: 3 readings 1 minute apart, average the last 2; repeat for at least 3 (preferably 7) days and discard day 1. Use ABPM to detect white-coat, masked and nocturnal hypertension.

BP above 180 systolic and/or 110 diastolic: refer the same day to exclude target organ damage and start treatment urgently, lowering BP gradually over hours to days (see hypertensive emergency protocol if organ damage is present).

sections.title: Work-up and organ damage
items: Essential: CBC, ECG (LVH, arrhythmia), urinalysis and urine albumin to creatinine ratio, creatinine and eGFR, urea and electrolytes, TSH, fasting glucose and HbA1c, lipid profile, and fundus examination.
Extended where available: echocardiography, renal ultrasound, ankle-brachial index, uric acid, Lp(a), carotid ultrasound, coronary calcium score.

Screen for secondary hypertension if onset before 40, resistant hypertension, abrupt loss of control, hypertensive crisis, hypokalaemia, adrenal mass, renal bruit, or organ damage out of proportion to BP: aldosterone to renin ratio, metanephrines, thyroid tests, renal ultrasound, urine protein.
Review drugs and products that raise BP at every visit: NSAIDs, steroids, oral contraceptives, sympathomimetics, energy drinks, high-sodium foods and supplements such as liquorice.

sections.title: When to treat and targets
items: Start drugs for confirmed BP of 140/90 or more (average of readings over 2 or more visits). Start above 130/80 if there is high cardiovascular risk, established CVD, CKD stage G3 or worse, diabetes with organ damage, or target organ damage.

Target for most adults on treatment: below 130/80 mmHg. With diabetes, CKD, coronary disease, previous stroke or heart failure: 120 to 129/70 to 79 mmHg if tolerated (below 140/80 in the elderly with CAD or stroke).
CKD: goal below 130/80, and systolic below 120 if well tolerated. Kidney transplant: below 130/80.

Frail elderly: start with a single drug at about half the standard dose, lower BP gradually over 1 to 2 months, and aim for office systolic 125 to 135 mmHg. Dihydropyridine CCBs and ACEI/ARBs are preferred for isolated systolic hypertension.
Achieving BP control matters more than the choice of drug class.

sections.title: Drug strategy
items: First-line classes: ACEI, ARB, calcium channel blocker, thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic, and beta-blocker (for angina, after MI, heart failure or rate control).
Start most patients on a low-dose two-drug single pill combination: an ACEI or ARB with a CCB or a thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic. Use single pill combinations at every step to improve adherence.
Not controlled at maximum tolerated doses: move to a three-drug combination of ACEI or ARB, CCB and thiazide-like diuretic.
Never combine two RAAS blockers (ACEI plus ARB): more hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury.

Coronary disease: ACEI or ARB plus a beta-blocker, aiming for heart rate 60 to 80/min; do not combine a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem. Stroke or TIA: ACEI, ARB or thiazide-type diuretic first.
Pregnancy or planning pregnancy: stop ACEI and ARB (see the pre-eclampsia protocol).

sections.title: Resistant hypertension
items: Resistant: BP above 140/90 despite at least 3 drugs of different classes at maximum tolerated doses, one a diuretic, with adherence confirmed and pseudoresistance (white-coat effect, poor technique) excluded by HBPM or ABPM.
Check adherence, salt intake, alcohol, interfering drugs and secondary causes; use a long-acting thiazide-like diuretic such as chlorthalidone with the ACEI or ARB and CCB.
Add spironolactone as the fourth drug if tolerated; finerenone is an option in CKD or hyperkalaemia risk when eGFR is 25 mL/min/1.73 m2 or more and potassium below 5.0 mmol/L.
Refer to a specialist hypertension centre; renal denervation may be considered if still uncontrolled.

sections.title: Monitoring and follow-up
items: Before starting: eGFR, creatinine, potassium and lying and standing BP. Orthostatic hypotension is a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic.
Review monthly (in person or virtually) for the first 3 months, and every 1 to 2 weeks while BP is above target. Use home BP monitoring for long-term follow-up.
A creatinine rise of up to 30% after starting an ACEI or ARB may be acceptable. Watch potassium in CKD, diabetes and with potassium-sparing drugs.

Side effects: ankle oedema and reflex tachycardia with dihydropyridine CCBs (less with an ACEI or ARB added); hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia with diuretics, especially in the elderly; cough with ACEI.
Annual review for every patient: BP control, adherence, side effects, and urine albumin to creatinine ratio, ECG and serum creatinine.

sections.title: Lifestyle for everyone
items: Sodium about 2 g a day (about 5 g of salt), and 1.5 to 2 g in diabetes or CKD; potassium-enriched salt substitutes are advised; limit packaged and processed foods and read labels.
DASH-type diet rich in fruit, vegetables and whole grains; regular physical activity; weight control.
Avoid alcohol and tobacco; if alcohol is taken, no more than 2 standard drinks a day for men and 1 to 1.5 for women (1 drink is about 10 g alcohol).

Stress reduction with controlled breathing, mindfulness or meditation. If serum uric acid is high with gout (above 6 mg/dL), treat with diet and urate-lowering drugs; losartan has a mild urate-lowering effect.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Diagnosing hypertension from a single office reading.
Starting with monotherapy and not titrating, instead of a two-drug single pill combination.
Using sublingual nifedipine or IV drugs to lower asymptomatic severe BP rapidly.
Combining an ACEI with an ARB.
Missing NSAIDs, steroids or high salt intake as the cause of poor control.

drugs.name: ACEI or ARB plus CCB or thiazide-like diuretic (single pill combination)
drugs.dose: Low-dose two-drug combination once daily, titrated to maximum tolerated doses
drugs.notes: Default first step for most adults (InSH 2025). InSH does not specify individual doses for routine use.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.dose: Add as fourth-line drug if tolerated
drugs.notes: Resistant hypertension; monitor potassium and creatinine.

drugs.name: Amlodipine
drugs.notes: Listed by InSH among oral options for severe hypertension without acute organ damage.

drugs.name: Labetalol (oral)
drugs.notes: Oral option for severe hypertension without acute organ damage.

drugs.name: Captopril
drugs.notes: Oral option for severe hypertension without acute organ damage; avoid in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Nifedipine extended release
drugs.notes: Never sublingual or immediate-release for rapid lowering.

sources.title: Indian Society of Hypertension (InSH) Consensus Guideline for the Management of Hypertension, 2025 (Hypertension Journal 11(4))
